post.description:
Issuance (issue #111's dial-in half, decided for #136). A bridge's identity is a token THIS control plane minted — that is what lets "who issued this identity?" have an answer at all, and it is the precondition the transport-inversion decision names for enabling a production bridge.
The control plane chooses the value with `crypto/rand` (32 bytes, rendered `cnd_<base64url>`). There is no way to register a value a caller supplies: the request names only the PARTY, and every field name an operator might reach for to smuggle one in — `credential`, `token`, `secret`, `verifier`, `verifier_sha256`, `verifier_env_name`, `digest_sha256` — is a declared honeypot that earns a 400 naming the offending field. Any OTHER unknown field is also refused (the decoder disallows unknown fields); the honeypots exist so the common mistake gets an explanation rather than a generic refusal.
REVEAL-ONCE, and it is structural rather than a convention:
- The plaintext lives in an `InboundCredentialSecret`, not a string.
  Its `String`, `GoString`, `MarshalJSON` and `LogValue` all render
  `[redacted inbound credential]`, so no `%v`, no `json.Marshal` and
  no log attribute can leak it.
- `Reveal()` returns the plaintext once, zeroes the backing buffer
  byte by byte, and drops it. A second `Reveal()` is an error.
- Only the SHA-256 digest is persistable — `IssuedInboundCredential`
  has no field the plaintext could occupy.
- There is NO read endpoint, on this API or any other, that can
  return the value again. This 201 response body is the only time it
  exists outside the minting process. Losing it means issuing a new
  one, which is the intended cost.
- The reveal happens only AFTER the verifier row commits: a
  credential handed out for a row that failed to write would be a
  secret nothing could verify.

Re-issuing for a party that already has a credential REPLACES it in place: the new verifier is stored, `verifier_env_name` is cleared, `issuance_count` increments, and `revoked_at`, `failure_count`, `locked_until` and the rate window are all RESET. The previous value stops admitting dials immediately, with nothing restarted — so re-issuance is also the way to clear a lockout.
The party key travels in the BODY, never the path: an actor key contains a slash (`namespace/name`), and a path-embedded key would be an escaping bug waiting to become a security bug.
Authenticated with its own bearer secret (`NODES_INBOUND_ISSUANCE_TOKEN_SECRET`) — NOT the dial-in headers a bridge uses, and not the decision or registration secrets. Issuing a bridge's identity is its own standing.

201.description: The credential was minted and the verifier is durable. This body carries the plaintext. It is the only time it will ever be returned.

400.description: The body did not decode, carried an unknown field, tried to supply credential material through one of the named honeypot fields, or named a party that is not a valid identity — `party_kind` outside {actor, host}, an actor key that is not `namespace/name`, or an address-shaped key (a dotted quad, or anything containing `:`), which is refused on shape so an address-like typo cannot become durable identity.

401.description: No bearer token was presented, it does not match the configured issuance secret, or no issuance secret is configured at all — closed by default, never mounted-but-authless.

post.summary: Mint one party's dial-in credential and reveal it exactly once.

post.description:
Revocation is scoped to exactly one (`party_kind`, `party_key`) row. No other bridge's session is touched and no process is restarted: the authenticator reads revocation state from PostgreSQL on every dial rather than caching it, so this takes effect on the revoked bridge's NEXT poll or completion and is unobservable to every other bridge.
It records rather than deletes. Deletion is not revocation — a restore or a replay could recreate a usable verifier — so the row survives carrying `revoked_at`, which is durable evidence of when authority ended. Re-revoking keeps the ORIGINAL instant: the fact being recorded is when authority ended, and that does not move.
Takes the same body and the same issuance bearer secret as `POST /v1alpha1/inbound/credentials`, including the honeypot refusals. To restore a revoked party, issue again — issuance clears `revoked_at`.

200.description: Authority has ended. `revoked_at` is the original revocation instant, which a re-revocation does not move.

400.description: Same refusals as issuance — undecodable body, unknown field, honeypot credential material, or an invalid/address-shaped party.

401.description: No bearer token, the wrong one, or no configured issuance secret.

404.description: No inbound credential exists for this party.

post.summary: End one party's dial-in authority.

post.description:
The claim half of the reverse transport (issue #150 documented what `internal/api/inbound_transport.go` has served since the transport inversion). The control plane holds no address for a bridge: the bridge dials OUT and asks for work, so this operation — not a dispatch to a participant URL — is how every unit of agent work reaches an agent.
Semantics, exactly as served:
- The request body is IGNORED. Bridges send an empty body; nothing is
  read, decoded or validated.
- A successful poll REFRESHES this actor's `last_seen_at` in
  `inbound_actor_presence` before it looks for work, which is the
  same fact `GET /v1alpha1/dial-in-presence` reads to answer
  "connected". Presence therefore tracks polling, not claiming: a
  bridge that polls for 25 idle seconds is connected.
- The mailbox is polled every 250ms for up to 25 SECONDS. The first
  claimable envelope for this actor key returns 200 immediately; the
  claim takes a 90-second lease (`claim_until`), after which an
  uncompleted envelope becomes claimable again by the next poll.
- When the 25 seconds elapse with nothing claimable the response is
  **204 with a completely EMPTY body** — not `{}`, not an Error
  envelope, not a 4xx. This is the single most load-bearing sentence
  on this operation. 204 is 2xx, so an HTTP client does NOT raise for
  it; a client that unconditionally parses the body will throw on
  `json.loads("")`, mistake a normal idle poll for a connection
  fault, and reconnect forever without ever claiming work. That is
  not hypothetical — it is the outage-shaped bug the shipped
  `dialin.py` now guards against explicitly (check `status == 204`
  OR an empty payload, then pause and re-poll).
- If the CLIENT disconnects mid-poll the server simply stops; no
  status is written and no work is claimed.

Authentication is per-bridge and takes BOTH headers together (see the `dial-in` tag): `X-Culture-Nodes-Actor-Key` names the party and `Authorization: Bearer` carries the credential this control plane issued for it. Both are checked on EVERY poll — the authenticator reads revocation, lockout and rate state from PostgreSQL per call and caches nothing, which is what makes revocation take effect on the next dial with nothing restarted.
The party kind is hardcoded to `actor` on this route. A `host`-kind credential (which `POST /v1alpha1/inbound/credentials` will happily mint) cannot dial in here.

200.description: One claimed mailbox envelope. The claim is already recorded when this is written, so an envelope returned here is leased to this bridge for 90 seconds whether or not it is ever completed.

204.description: The long poll expired with nothing claimable. The body is EMPTY — zero bytes. Do not attempt to parse it; pause briefly and poll again.

401.description:
The dial was refused. `X-Culture-Nodes-Actor-Key` was absent, or the authenticator returned one of the named refusal reasons (`invalid_credential`, `revoked`, `not_control_plane_issued`, `locked_out`, `rate_limited` — see the `dial-in` tag).
NOTE: unlike every other operation in this API, this body is `text/plain`, not the Error schema — the route is not mounted through the wrapper that renders Error. It reads `dial-in refused: <reason>` or `dial-in authentication is not configured`.

500.description: The presence touch, the authentication state read, or the mailbox claim failed. This one IS the Error schema — store failures on this route go through the standard renderer even though the 401 above does not.

post.summary: Long-poll for one unit of work addressed to this bridge.

post.description:
The settle half of the reverse transport. The bridge forwards the envelope's `request` to its own local invocation handler, then posts whatever that handler answered — status line and body, verbatim — back here. The control plane is waiting synchronously on exactly this row: `InvokeInbound` polls `inbound_actor_mailbox` for `completed_at IS NOT NULL` and then parses `{status, body}` as the invocation response, so a completion is the dispatch's return value, not a notification about it.
`id` is the envelope's `id` from the poll response — NOT its `attempt_id`. The two are different identifiers and only one of them addresses this route.
A completion is scoped to the claiming actor: the UPDATE is keyed on (`id`, namespace, actor key, `completed_at IS NULL`), so one bridge cannot complete another's envelope and no envelope completes twice.
Both dial-in headers are required again, and are re-authenticated from durable state on this call as well — a credential revoked while the bridge was working is refused here even though the poll that handed out the work succeeded.

parameters.description: The envelope id from the poll response's `id` field. Not `attempt_id`.
parameters.name: id

204.description: The envelope is settled and the waiting dispatch has its response. Empty body.

400.description:
The body did not decode as JSON (including a body over the 8 MiB limit), or `status` was outside 100-599, or `body` was absent.
Like the poll's 401, this body is `text/plain`, not the Error schema: `invalid completion`, or `status and body are required`.

401.description: The dial was refused — same header requirements, same named reasons, and same `text/plain` body as `POST /v1alpha1/inbound/poll`.

500.description: The Error schema. Documented as 500 because that is what the route actually returns, including for the caller-caused case of an envelope id that is unknown, belongs to another actor, or was already completed — the store returns a plain error there, so it is rendered as an unclassified environment failure rather than a 404 or a 409. That is a known wart in the implementation, not a gap in this description.

post.summary: Return one claimed envelope's response to the control plane.

The cross-run "jobs timeline" listing (task t11): every node run in this namespace, not scoped to one run — unlike the `node_runs` nested in GET /v1alpha1/runs/{id}'s Run-view payload — newest-first by `updated_at`, using `node_runs_namespace_updated_at_idx` (migrations/0010) for the namespace scope, the `updated_since`/`updated_until` range, and the sort in one index walk.

Pagination is a keyset cursor (`cursor`/`next_cursor`), not OFFSET: `updated_at` changes on every node run's state transition — including rows outside the caller's current page — so an OFFSET-based page would silently skip or repeat rows as items elsewhere in the namespace move past the offset boundary between two requests. A cursor anchored to `(updated_at, id)` of the last row already served has no such failure mode and reuses the same index walk a first page already does. Pass `next_cursor` from a response back as `cursor` to fetch the next page; its absence means there is no further page.

get.description:
Answers "what is awaiting my decision", per run and across runs, without a hand-maintained manifest of run ids.
A record is pending when it carries `proposed` authority and no `review` record names it as its subject — whatever the verdict would have been, since a rejection answers the question as completely as a confirmation does. It is NOT simply `authority = proposed`: records are immutable, so committing a confirmation appends a review record rather than changing the claim, and a decided claim reads `proposed` forever. A record a later record supersedes is excluded too — the correction that replaced it is what should be decided now.
Results are grouped by run and each group carries that run's current `ledger_version`, which is exactly what POST /v1alpha1/runs/{id}/reviews needs to open a review over them.
An unrecognised query parameter is refused with 400 rather than ignored: a filter silently dropped answers a different question than the one asked while still looking authoritative.

Each item is the lightweight summary shape (no `tasks`/`deviations` — those are read one snapshot at a time via `GET /v1alpha1/plan-imports/{id}`, since an empty array here would misread as "zero tasks" rather than "not fetched on this path").

get.description:
Task t14 (issue #67): the clarify-then-commit gate's read surface. An actor whose registration enables the gate (`metadata.preflight_gate`) is briefed BEFORE its first billable turn: the worker composes the operating facts its task depends on — the host capabilities that actor's own bridge advertised, plus the task declaration — appends them as a `derived` ledger record, and defers the dispatch until the briefing is acknowledged.

This endpoint answers "is anything waiting on me". The issue also goes onto the run's event stream (`dev.culture.nodes.dispatch.preflight_issued`), but a bridge that was not watching at that instant would otherwise never learn, so the pending set is queryable. Only PENDING preflights are listed — unconsumed, unanswered and unexpired; one preflight's own history stays readable at its detail route.

An actor cannot acknowledge what it cannot read, so the document is always part of the detail response: the host capabilities as its bridge advertised them, the task declaration, the expected terminal shape, and the refusal stating what does not proceed until it is acknowledged.

post.description:
The second, separate action of clarify-then-commit. It appends the acknowledging actor's `proposed` `dispatch_acknowledgement` record — naming the briefing by id AND by content digest — and marks the row, after which exactly ONE dispatch may ride it.

The properties are the ones `deploy/prod/install-secrets.sh`'s destructive-confirmation protocol established and this generalizes from danger to understanding: it is SINGLE-USE (the next dispatch of that node needs its own briefing) and WINDOWED (an acknowledgement made too long ago authorizes nothing). Both refusals are 409s naming the state.

What it writes is a CLAIM, not evidence: an actor saying it understood is a completion-claim-shaped statement, and nothing on this path promotes it (PRD §10.4). `actor_id` names the actor the acknowledgement is recorded FOR; the record's `origin` names the producer that wrote it, so an operator acknowledging on a bridge's behalf stays distinguishable afterwards.

post.description:
Applies confirm/reject decisions for every record the review named, all in one transaction, or none (PRD §10.8). Refused — with nothing written — when the caller's expected ledger version no longer matches: the ledger moved, a reviewed record was superseded, or the reviewed frame no longer checksums to what was requested.
Each decision is appended as its own immutable `review` record: human origin naming the reviewer, `confirmed` or `rejected` authority, `subject_ref` naming the record decided, and the stated `rationale` in its payload. post.description:
The merge gate expressed as a NODE (task t16, issue #101). Where `suite-verdicts` records one suite's exit code, this records every gate a workflow declared — the ones that ran and the ones that did not — plus an aggregate the control plane computes over them.

A gate that RAN is composed through exactly the same `handover.SuiteVerdict` the single-suite endpoint uses, so its record is identical to the one an operator's `scripts/collect-handover.py --gate` writes today, with the gate matrix's own annotations (`gate`, `instrument`, `value`, `unit`, `threshold`) added.

A gate that did NOT run states `not_applicable` with a reason from a closed vocabulary and the changed files it left uncovered. Its record carries NO `verdict` key at all: no verdict was reached, and writing one would make an unmeasured gate sortable beside measured ones. This is the shape `suite-verdicts` cannot express — there, `exit_code` is required precisely so a malformed request cannot become a pass, which leaves no way to say "this instrument never reached the change".

Per gate, exactly ONE of `exit_code` and `not_applicable` is accepted. Naming both, or neither, is refused: those are the two shapes in which an unmeasured gate could pass itself off as a measured one.

The aggregate's four counts (`declared`, `applicable`, `passed`, `failed`, `not_applicable`) and its outcome are COMPUTED from the statuses in the request — there is no field for either. That is what stops an empty scan from looking green: a report in which no gate was applicable yields `measurement_incomplete`, never `gates_passed`, and so does a report in which any instrument was unavailable on the host that ran it.

The route is gated by the same bearer secret as the review surface, and `validator_actor_id` must be a registered non-human actor, for the reasons `suite-verdicts` states.

201.description:
Every gate landed as a derived, validator-origin review record, followed by the aggregate — whose `provenance_refs` name each record it counted, so the derivation can be re-performed rather than believed.

Each REJECTING gate is also routed through the same bounded repair routing a singly-posted verdict gets (task t32, issue #102): two repair attempts per run over a 24-hour window, both ceilings reaching a human. Nothing is dispatched.

post.description:
The merge gate's mechanical half (task t11, issue #101). A test suite is a DETERMINISTIC VALIDATOR — a commit plus a command produces a number — so PRD §10.4 admits its finding as a `derived` record, with the validator named in `validator_actor_id` as its origin. That is the whole point of the endpoint: an operator reading a green tick and deciding to merge leaves nothing behind that names the suite, the exit code, or the commit, and is not evidence of anything.

Three refusals are load-bearing. `exit_code` is REQUIRED and is never defaulted, because an omitted exit code silently meaning 0 would turn every malformed request into a pass. `commit_sha` must be a full 40-character lowercase hex commit id — not `HEAD`, not a branch name, not an abbreviation — because a verdict that does not name what it tested cannot be checked later. And when the control plane has already MEASURED this run's handover (an observed evidence record from a `git_ref_fetch`), a verdict naming a different commit is refused outright rather than recorded with a caveat.

`validator_actor_id` must be a registered actor and must not be one registered as `human`: a person who ran a suite and reported the result is making a claim about it, which is the mirror of the reviewer-must-be-human rule the review surface enforces. The route is gated by the same bearer secret as the review surface — whoever can record a suite verdict can decide a merge.

201.description:
The verdict was recorded as a derived, validator-origin review record. Its `subject_ref` and `provenance_refs` name the run's handover evidence record when the control plane had measured one, and are empty when it had not.

A REJECTING verdict is also ROUTED (task t32, issue #102): the control plane derives where the failure goes next — a bounded repair attempt on a lane whose advertised capability surface shows it can run the suite that failed, or a human — and appends that decision as a second derived record, returned as `routing`. The bound is stated in the record: two repair attempts per run, over a 24-hour window measured from the run's first gate rejection, and a human node at either ceiling.

The routing is a DECISION, not an execution: nothing is dispatched, and the record says so in its own payload. Unattended repair is deliberately not enabled — see the record's `dispatch_note`.

tags.description:
The reverse transport, and the credential lane that admits it. The control plane stores no address for a bridge — the bridge dials OUT, claims work from a durable mailbox, and posts the result back — so these four operations are the write side of the same lane GET /v1alpha1/dial-in-presence reads.
Two DIFFERENT authentications live here, and confusing them is the easiest mistake to make against this API:
- The transport (`/v1alpha1/inbound/poll`,
  `/v1alpha1/inbound/{id}/complete`) authenticates a BRIDGE, and needs
  both headers on every call: `X-Culture-Nodes-Actor-Key: <namespace>/<name>`
  naming the party, and `Authorization: Bearer <credential>` carrying
  the `cnd_`-prefixed value this control plane issued for it.
- Issuance and revocation (`/v1alpha1/inbound/credentials`,
  `/v1alpha1/inbound/credentials/revoke`) authenticate an OPERATOR,
  with one bearer secret and no actor-key header at all.

A bridge's dial is refused with one of five named reasons, evaluated in this order under a per-credential lock:
- `revoked` — authority was ended by the revoke operation. Checked
  first, so a revoked credential is refused before anything else.
- `not_control_plane_issued` — a verifier record exists but this
  control plane did not MINT it (a hand-inserted digest, or a
  `verifier_env_name` pointing at an operator-invented token). This is
  a property of the RECORD, not of what was presented, so it is
  answered before lockout and before the rate window and consumes
  neither — the answer cannot vary with the presentation, so refusing
  early discloses nothing. On by default
  (`RequireControlPlaneIssued`); a deployment wanting the older
  operator-provisioned record must ask for it explicitly.
- `locked_out` — 5 consecutive bad presentations lock the credential
  for 15 minutes. Carries the retry instant. A successful
  authentication clears the counter; so does re-issuing.
- `rate_limited` — at most 10 presentations per credential per
  60-second window, GOOD OR BAD. Deliberately separate from lockout,
  so neither control stands in for the other. Carries the instant the
  window reopens.
- `invalid_credential` — the presented value does not verify. Only
  this one increments the failure counter.

Every refusal renders as 401. The decision object carries no credential material by construction.
